displayQuote: Television Is Chewing Gum for the Eyes

meta.title: Who really said "Television Is Chewing Gum for the Eyes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Frank Lloyd Wright's coinage. Yale's Henri Peyre wrote it in 1944 about movies and radio; critic John Mason Brown moved it to television in 1955.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Television Is Chewing Gum for the Eyes'?
meta.ogDescription: Wright repeated it in 1958; he didn't coin it. The metaphor is Henri Peyre's, printed in 1944 — and even John Mason Brown refused the credit.

answer.label: Not Frank Lloyd Wright — the metaphor is Henri Peyre’s
answer.authorDates: 1901–1988 · French-born literary scholar, Sterling Professor of French at Yale
answer.sourceLine: The image is in print eleven years before anyone aimed it at television: Henri Peyre’s Writers and Their Critics: A Study of Misunderstanding (Cornell University Press, 1944), page 291, where dulled adults absorb “the chewing gum for the eyes of the movies or the chewing gum for the ears of the radio.” Drama critic John Mason Brown moved it to the new medium in a January 1955 interview — and even he refused the credit, telling one anthologist he had the line from “a friend of his small son.” Wright very likely did use it, at a Chicago dinner reported in January 1958, but that is the earliest trace of him anywhere near it: he repeated a line already three years old on television and fourteen years old in print.

source.heading: The 1944 sentence the line grew out of

docMeta.dd: Writers and Their Critics: A Study of Misunderstanding
Henri Peyre, Sterling Professor of French in Yale University
Cornell University Press, Ithaca, New York, 1944 — page 291
John Mason Brown, interviewed by Steven H. Scheur, Syracuse Herald-Journal, 21 January 1955

source.excerpt: Yet there is no sorrier sight to watch then the vacant faces of those former high school and college students when, at thirty-five or fifty, all their mental alertness having vanished, the spark gone from their eyes, they dutifully chew their gum to keep from yawning, while absorbing the chewing gum for the eyes of the movies or the chewing gum for the ears of the radio. The same men who once read Shakespeare, Molière, Byron glance at the headlines of their tabloid papers, turn straight to the page of the funnies, to devour them with the same dutiful sense of boredom as they swallow their hamburger at lunchtime and their highball after dinner.
trail: 1944 — Yale’s Henri Peyre describes readers gone slack “absorbing the chewing gum for the eyes of the movies or the chewing gum for the ears of the radio,” on page 291 of Writers and Their Critics. Confirmed directly in the scanned Cornell University Press first edition ↗. Television is not in the sentence.

January 1955 — drama critic John Mason Brown moves the metaphor to the new medium, telling film critic Steven H. Scheur that “so much of TV seems to be chewing gum for the eyes.” Six months later he told anthologist James Beasley Simpson he had the line from “a friend of his small son.” Both citations are set out by Quote Investigator ↗.

January 1958 — Ed Sullivan’s syndicated column reports Frank Lloyd Wright using the line at a Chicago dinner. That is the earliest ascription to Wright Quote Investigator ↗ has located — three years after Brown, fourteen after Peyre, and a little over a year before Wright’s death in April 1959.

2013 — quotation researcher Garson O’Toole posts the 1944 antedating to the American Dialect Society list, noting that the Yale Book of Quotations had dated the phrase to 28 July 1955 ↗ — the Brown interview, eleven years too late.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned Cornell University Press first edition; the page number is confirmed by the running head “Toward a Reconciliation 291.” The sentence really does read “no sorrier sight to watch then” — an uncorrected slip for “than” in the 1944 printing, kept here rather than tidied. Note what is missing: Peyre is describing movies and radio. The word “television” does not appear.

source.rightsNote: The passage shown is from Writers and Their Critics: A Study of Misunderstanding, first published by Cornell University Press in 1944 — well after the 1931 boundary for the United States public domain, so it should be treated as still in copyright and quoted only in brief. The popular one-line television version carries no clean rights status of its own: John Mason Brown, who first aimed it at television in 1955, credited an unnamed young person rather than himself, so that wording has no identified author to hold rights in it.

author.name: Henri Peyre
author.heading: Who was Henri Peyre?
author.metaLine: 1901–1988 · French-born literary scholar; Sterling Professor of French at Yale, 1938–1969
author.bio: Henri Maurice Peyre was a French-born American scholar of literature who held Yale’s Sterling Professorship of French from 1938 until 1969, making him one of the most influential interpreters of French writing in the English-speaking world. Writers and Their Critics: A Study of Misunderstanding (1944) is his argument about why authors and critics talk past one another — and the chewing-gum line is not a thesis in it but a throwaway aside, buried in a section headed “Toward a Reconciliation,” complaining that mass entertainment had gone soft in the mouths of people who once read Shakespeare. He was writing about movies and radio. Television, in 1944, was barely a product.

copyAttribution: "Television is chewing gum for the eyes." — commonly credited to Frank Lloyd Wright, but not his coinage. The metaphor is Henri Peyre's, in Writers and Their Critics: A Study of Misunderstanding (Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 1944), 291, where it describes movies and radio rather than television. Drama critic John Mason Brown applied it to television by 21 January 1955 and credited an unnamed young person, not himself. The earliest ascription to Wright is Ed Sullivan's column of 10 January 1958. Chronology: Quote Investigator, "Quote Origin: Television Is Chewing Gum for the Eyes."

misattribution.heading: Three famous names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This is a quotation that has been passed hand to hand for eighty years, picking up a more famous owner at nearly every stop. Here is who gets credited, and what the paper trail actually supports.

items.why: The earliest link between Wright and the line that Quote Investigator ↗ can find is Ed Sullivan’s newspaper column of 10 January 1958, reporting that Wright used it at a Chicago dinner — three years after the line was already circulating on television and fourteen years after it appeared in print. Wright very likely did say it; there is no evidence he invented it, and no version of it appears on his Wikiquote page ↗ at all.

items.tag: Sourceless — and the dates are wrong
items.why: Aggregators print the line under Wright’s name with no citation of any kind. The Quotations Page ↗ is typical: “TV is chewing gum for the eyes,” no source, and a birth year of 1869 — Wright was born on 8 June 1867 ↗. A page that cannot get the man’s birth year right is not evidence about his sentences.

Dick Cavett wrote in New York Magazine in 1974 that “Fred Allen called TV chewing gum for the eyes.” Allen was a plausible candidate — a radio comic famous for hating television — but Quote Investigator ↗ reports the ascription as “not well-supported,” with no earlier trace connecting Allen to the phrase.

items.scope: The man usually named as the real source
items.why: Brown is the one who put the metaphor on television, from January 1955, and Time credited him with it as late as 1968. But he never claimed it. Interviewed by anthologist James Beasley Simpson on 28 July 1955 he presented it as something he was quoting from “a friend of his small son,” and Walter Winchell’s October 1955 column has him crediting “a young man of 17 but of great wisdom” — both recorded by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The metaphor belongs to Henri Peyre, who published it in 1944 about movies and radio — verifiable on page 291 of the scanned first edition ↗. John Mason Brown aimed it at television in 1955 while insisting the words were someone else’s. Frank Lloyd Wright, so far as the record shows, simply said it well and said it loudly.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Wright
lead: A line needs a mouth. “Chewing gum for the eyes” spent its first decade in the wrong one: a Yale professor of French, in a scholarly book about literary criticism, aiming at the movies. Nobody repeats a professor. When John Mason Brown — a famous, quotable drama critic with a column in the Saturday Review — pointed it at television in 1955, it started to travel, and by that June Time was printing it. But Brown kept handing the credit away: to “a friend of his small son,” to “a young man of 17 but of great wisdom.” A quip with no owner is an orphan looking for a famous parent.

It found one in January 1958, when Ed Sullivan’s column reported Frank Lloyd Wright using it at a Chicago dinner. Wright was the perfect host: ninety, ferociously quotable, and openly contemptuous of the culture around him. Within six weeks a Chicago Tribune columnist was printing it as “Definition of television from Frank Lloyd Wright.” By that October a West Virginia paper was already sour about it, grumbling that “some poor press agent has succeeded in getting his client credit with saying” the line. That is the whole mechanism, visible in nine months of newsprint: a good line drifts uphill toward the most famous name in the room.
detailsBody: 1944 — Henri Peyre, Writers and Their Critics, p. 291: the chewing gum for the eyes of the movies, and for the ears of the radio. 21 January 1955 — John Mason Brown, interviewed by film critic Steven H. Scheur in the Syracuse Herald-Journal: “So much of TV seems to be chewing gum for the eyes.” June 1955 — Time reports Brown saying it on the radio programme “Invitation to Learning.” 28 July 1955 — Brown repeats it to anthologist James Beasley Simpson, crediting “a friend of his small son”; this is the date the Yale Book of Quotations later used. October 1955 — Walter Winchell prints Brown’s version, credited to an anonymous seventeen-year-old.

10 January 1958 — Ed Sullivan’s column carries the first known Wright ascription. February 1958 — the Chicago Tribune repeats it as Wright’s. April 1959 — the Washington Post, reviewing Wright’s career after his death, calls it “the remark credited to him.” 1960 — Bennett Cerf gives Wright a mutated form, “chewing gum for the eyeballs.” 1968 — Time swings back and credits Brown. 1974 — Dick Cavett, in New York Magazine, credits comedian Fred Allen instead. Quote Investigator finds no support for the Allen version.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the metaphor to Henri Peyre's 1944 Writers and Their Critics (movies and radio), records John Mason Brown applying it to television in January 1955 and crediting an unnamed young person, identifies Ed Sullivan's 10 January 1958 column as the earliest ascription to Frank Lloyd Wright, and calls the Fred Allen ascription 'not well-supported'.

The scanned Cornell University Press first edition of Henri Peyre's Writers and Their Critics: A Study of Misunderstanding (1944) contains, on the page whose running head reads 'Toward a Reconciliation 291', the words 'while absorbing the chewing gum for the eyes of the movies or the chewing gum for the ears of the radio', and its title page reads 'HENRI PEYRE, Sterling Professor of French in Yale University / Ithaca, New York / CORNELL UNIVERSITY PRESS / 1944'.

Garson O'Toole posted to the American Dialect Society list on 13 September 2013 documenting Peyre's 1944 usage and John Mason Brown's 21 January 1955 television usage, and noting that the Yale Book of Quotations cites the phrase to 28 July 1955.
Henri Maurice Peyre lived 21 February 1901 to 9 December 1988, was a French-born American scholar, and held the Sterling Professorship of French at Yale from 1938 to 1969.

John Mason Brown (3 July 1900 – 16 March 1969) was an American drama critic and author whose 'Seeing Things' column appeared in the Saturday Review from 1944 until his death, and the page associates him with the phrase 'chewing gum for the eyes'.
Wikiquote's Frank Lloyd Wright page does not contain 'chewing gum for the eyes' in any section — not in Quotes, Attributed, Misattributed, or Quotes about Wright.
The Quotations Page presents 'TV is chewing gum for the eyes.' credited to 'Frank Lloyd Wright, US architect (1869 - 1959)' with no publication source or original context given.
Frank Lloyd Wright was born 8 June 1867 and died 9 April 1959, and was an American architect, designer, writer, and educator.
